intro:
Serracapriola, one of the most fascinating villages in Daunia, is a place where history and legend intertwine. Many stories have been passed down orally for centuries and are part of the town's identity, even if they don't always have a historical basis.

Here are some of the most evocative tales.
s1_titolo: The Legend of the Roe Deer and the Madonna
s1_testo:
This is the most famous legend of the village.

It is said that a count, during a hunting trip, chased a roe deer that seemed to be luring him to a specific spot in the forest. The animal stopped in front of a small cave and disappeared. Entering the cavity, the count found an altar with an image of the Virgin Mary.

Interpreting the episode as a divine sign, he had a small church built dedicated to Santa Maria in Silvis. Around that sanctuary, the village would later be born, taking the name "Serra Capriola", meaning the hill of the roe deer. Historians believe, however, that the name may have a Roman origin linked to the surname Capreolus, while the legend remains a much-loved popular explanation.
s2_titolo: The Witches and Father Matteo d'Agnone
s2_testo:
Serracapriola is deeply connected to the figure of Father Matteo d'Agnone.

Tradition tells that he continuously fought the devil and witches. Numerous episodes narrate exorcisms, apparitions and confrontations with evil. Even today, during some religious celebrations, the elders remember these stories as part of the collective memory of the village.
s3_titolo: The Castle and the Secret Passages
s3_testo:
As with many medieval castles, the one in Serracapriola is surrounded by mysterious tales.

According to popular tradition, underneath the castle there would be underground tunnels that allowed the lords of the fief to escape during sieges or secretly reach the church and other buildings in the village. There is no evidence to confirm all these passages, but the legend continues to fascinate visitors and residents alike.
s4_titolo: The Souls of the Ancient Village
s4_testo:
Walking through the oldest alleyways, some say they have heard footsteps or voices in the silent nights.

These are stories probably born from the atmosphere of the medieval historic center, with its narrow lanes, ancient stone houses and the castle lit by the moon. It is the classic folklore that accompanies many Italian villages.
s5_testo:
Until a few decades ago, beliefs in the evil eye, amulets against bad luck and rituals to protect crops and animals were widespread.

These traditions blended with popular religiosity and the feasts dedicated to San Mercurio and the Madonna, creating a heritage of customs still remembered today in local celebrations.
s6_testo:
The inhabitants of Serracapriola often say that the village "lives with two souls": the historical one, made of castles, knights and feudal lords, and the mystical one, linked to saints, exorcists and tales of the supernatural. This combination makes the village one of the richest in folklore in northern Puglia.

If you are interested in mystery, I can also tell you the most intriguing stories of Serracapriola, including those about the castle's ghosts, witchcraft tales and ancient popular beliefs handed down by the elders.
s7_testo:
This is one of the most chilling stories.

In the castle courtyard there is a deep opening, called by tradition the trabocchetto (trapdoor). According to legend it was not a simple well: whoever fell in was dragged into a clever mechanism that crushed their bones. There is no evidence that such a device ever existed, but the tale is still one of the most famous in the village.
s8_testo: Inside the castle there is a small chapel built, according to tradition, after a tragic episode in the 18th century. The story speaks of a crime that shook the feudal family, and for this reason an altar was erected to atone for the guilt. From here comes the belief that some rooms of the castle are "charged" with presences and memories.
s9_testo:
Farmers used to tell of seeing, on summer nights, small blue lights floating among the fields towards the Fortore river.

For some they were souls in torment; others said they pointed to hidden old treasures. Today we know that similar phenomena can be explained by natural gases or optical illusions, but the tale has remained in local folklore.
s10_testo:
When the Benedictines left Serracapriola, according to popular tradition they hid a treasure of coins and sacred objects that was never found.

Many believe the hoard is still buried under some building in the historic center or in the castle's underground passages. There are no documents to confirm this story, but it is a legend widespread in many families of the village.
s11_testo:
It is not just one secret passage that is spoken of.

Tradition holds that beneath Serracapriola there exists a whole network of galleries connecting the castle, Santa Maria in Silvis and even some farmhouses outside the village. So far the existence of such an extensive system has never been proven, but the myth continues to fuel the imagination.
s12_testo:
Even a real episode has taken on almost epic proportions.

On 1 October 1943, during the German retreat, the inhabitants rose up against the Nazis. The action cost eleven lives and the village was even remembered by Radio London as the "heroic little town of Capitanata". Over time this episode has entered the collective memory almost like a modern legend.
s13_testo:
The elders of Serracapriola used to say that one must not whistle at night near the castle, because the whistle would "call" the spirits or attract bad luck. It is a superstition typical of southern Italy that remained alive in the village until a few decades ago, even though it does not appear in official records.

If you enjoy these tales, I can also tell you the darkest and most frightening legends of the Gargano and Daunia, some truly spine-chilling.
s14_testo: It was said that, on nights of the full moon, a knight slowly crossed the old village heading towards the castle. He wore ancient armour, but no one could see his face. Those who met him had to remain silent: greeting him would bring misfortune for a year. He left no footprints nor the sound of horse hooves.
s15_testo: When the Benedictines left Serracapriola, legend has it they hid a treasure of coins, relics and ancient manuscripts. The location would be indicated by strange symbols carved in stone, but no one has ever managed to interpret them. Even today some claim the treasure is hidden beneath the historic center. The Benedictines' presence is historically documented, while the treasure belongs to popular tradition.
s16_testo: Farmers used to tell that, during summer nights, small blue lights could be seen moving among the fields around the village. For some they were souls in torment, for others they pointed to the spot where an ancient treasure was hidden. Out of caution, no one ever came close.
s17_testo: Near the ancient walls, according to a popular belief, there was a stone that had to be touched before setting off on a long journey. Anyone who brushed it would always return home safe and sound. Many emigrants, before leaving Serracapriola, said they had stopped there.
s18_titolo: The Bells That Rang on Their Own
s18_testo: The elders told that, on the occasion of great calamities or the death of very important people, the church bells would begin to vibrate or ring without anyone having moved them. It was considered a divine sign inviting the inhabitants to pray.
s19_testo: There was a saying that the wind blowing from the Serra "spoke". On winter evenings, its whistling between the houses seemed to turn into voices. The oldest people said they were the memories of the ancestors returning to protect the village.
s20_testo: A young noblewoman, betrothed against her will, is said to have died of grief within the castle walls. Since then, on silent nights, some swear they see a figure dressed in white appearing at a window on the piano nobile and disappearing shortly after. It is a typical ghost legend with no historical confirmation, but one that fits perfectly into the imagery linked to Castello Maresca.
